terms.gloss: thought, the mind’s power of picturing
evidence: Auct. Her. 3.32: cōgitātiō enim quamvīs regiōnem potest amplectī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Classical prose has no single word for the faculty; it says “thought” and “the mind”: cōgitātiōne fingere, animō fingere (see imagine). Its everyday sense is simply thinking or a thought.
Imagination as the gift of invention: a person’s natural cast of mind, wit, talent. Not the picturing faculty.

evidence: Tac. Ann. 15.36: prōvinciās sēcrētīs imāginātiōnibus agitāns (Lewis & Short)
M-O s.v. imagination: a mental picture
terms.comment: A thing imagined, a fancy, rather than the faculty; Augustine uses it more freely (Conf. 7.5).
Greek; Cicero writes it in Greek and translates it vīsum (Lewis & Short). Petronius’s phantasia, nōn homō (38) is a mere figment of a man.

phrases.latin: fingite animīs — līberae sunt enim nostrae cōgitātiōnēs et quae volunt sīc intuentur ut ea cernimus quae vidēmus
phrases.english: imagine it — for our thoughts are free, and they see what they wish as plainly as we see what is before our eyes

sources: Lewis & Short: cogitatio · Lewis & Short: ingenium · Lewis & Short: imaginatio · Lewis & Short: phantasia
Morgan–Owens, Adumbratio: s.vv. imagination, imagination: a mental picture, imagination: creativity.
Cicero’s Pro Milone as quoted in the record imagine.
